RP_INTRO_ARGUMENT.label: Introduction argument
RP_INTRO_ARGUMENT.purpose: Reconstruct the argument an Introduction makes for its contribution. What the authors assert is author-asserted, not verified.
RP_INTRO_ARGUMENT.instructions: Read the text and report only what the authors themselves state. For every record, quote the exact words that carry it. Do not judge whether the argument is correct, and do not supply a component the authors did not state.

fields.name: phenomenon
fields.description: the problem or phenomenon the paper says needs explaining

fields.name: established_knowledge
fields.description: what the authors say prior work has shown or explained

fields.name: unresolved_tension
fields.description: the disagreement, limitation, untested assumption or open question the authors identify

fields.name: proposed_contribution
fields.description: what the authors say the paper adds, changes or bounds (give `type` when the authors' wording makes it clear)

fields.name: evidence_needed
fields.description: the evidence or tests the authors say are needed to defend the contribution

RP_THEORY.label: Theory and mechanism
RP_THEORY.purpose: Record the theory a paper invokes, the mechanism it assumes, how it defines its constructs and which assumptions it tests.
RP_THEORY.instructions: Report only what the paper states. Quote construct definitions verbatim. If the paper does not state an assumption or a mechanism, leave the field out and list it under gaps; do not infer one. Conceptual papers name their sections after their ideas: read every section that is shown, not only the ones called theory.

fields.name: theory_invoked
fields.description: the theory or theoretical framing the paper relies on (put its name in `label`)

fields.name: assumed_mechanism
fields.description: the mechanism the paper assumes links its constructs (put its name in `label`)

fields.name: construct_definition
fields.description: a construct as the paper defines it (quote the definition; put the construct's name in `label`)

fields.name: stated_assumption
fields.description: an assumption the paper states

fields.name: assumption_tested
fields.description: an assumption the paper says it tests

RP_METHOD.label: Method record
RP_METHOD.purpose: Record how a study was done, as candidate input to a method playbook. Fidelity to the source is checked before anything is reused.
RP_METHOD.instructions: Report each design choice the paper states, with the words that state it. Do not complete a procedure from general knowledge of the method. A choice the paper does not state is a gap. Each `value` restates only what its own `quote` says. If a detail you want is in another sentence, make a second record whose quote is that sentence; never merge two sentences into one value, and never add an example, a name or a number that is not in the quote.

fields.name: study_design
fields.description: the research design or type of study

fields.name: sample_selection
fields.description: how the sample or data were selected, including filters and exclusions

fields.name: label_construction
fields.description: how the outcome or label was defined and where it comes from

fields.name: variable_measurement
fields.description: how a variable or feature is measured

fields.name: model_or_estimator
fields.description: the model, estimator or algorithm used

fields.name: validation_or_tests
fields.description: how results are validated, tested or compared (splits, baselines, tests)

fields.name: interpretation_rule
fields.description: how the paper says estimates or scores should be interpreted

fields.name: limitation_handling
fields.description: how the paper addresses a limitation or threat

RP_CONTRIBUTION.label: Contribution record
RP_CONTRIBUTION.purpose: Record what a paper says it contributes, and on which explicit dimensions it can be compared with a focus study.
RP_CONTRIBUTION.instructions: Report what the authors state about their question, design, setting, mechanism and contribution. Their statement of contribution is author-asserted. Quote the words; do not summarise beyond them.

fields.name: research_question
fields.description: the question the paper asks

fields.name: design
fields.description: the design or approach, as stated

fields.name: setting
fields.description: the setting, sample or context, as stated

fields.name: mechanism
fields.description: the mechanism the paper proposes or tests

fields.name: claimed_contribution
fields.description: what the paper says it contributes

RP_LANDSCAPE.label: Landscape record
RP_LANDSCAPE.purpose: Record what a paper reports, argues, assumes, measures and admits, as entries of a landscape of the literature on a problem. A paper may be empirical, interpretive or conceptual: record only the kind of claim it actually makes. The landscape compares papers; it never decides which of them is right.
RP_LANDSCAPE.instructions: Report only what the paper states, with the words that state it. Each `value` restates only what its own `quote` says: no number, name or condition that is not in the quote. For an empirical `finding`, put a short name for the relationship or quantity it concerns in `label` (for example "detection model use -> manipulation"; use the same name for the same relationship wherever it appears) and its direction in `type`: positive, negative, null (no effect found), mixed or descriptive. For a `theoretical_claim` (a proposition, the conclusion of an argument, a critique of earlier work or a proposed reconceptualisation) name the idea it concerns in `label` and say which kind it is in `type`. For an `interpretive_finding` (a theme, pattern or interpretation the authors derive from qualitative material) name it in `label`. Use a field only when the paper makes that kind of claim: do not turn an argument into a finding or a finding into an argument. Do not compare the paper with other papers, do not say whether a claim is credible, and do not complete an assumption or a limitation the paper does not state; what it does not state is a gap.

fields.name: finding
fields.description: a result the paper reports, with the population, period or estimand the sentence states

fields.name: theoretical_claim
fields.description: a claim a conceptual or theoretical paper argues for: a proposition, the conclusion of an argument, a critique of earlier work, or a proposed reconceptualisation

fields.name: interpretive_finding
fields.description: an interpretation, theme or pattern the authors derive from qualitative material, as the sentence states it

fields.name: boundary_condition
fields.description: where the paper says a finding does not hold, or holds only under a stated condition

fields.name: identifying_assumption
fields.description: an assumption the paper's design relies on; type says whether the paper tests it

fields.name: measurement
fields.description: the measure or proxy used for a construct (name the construct in `label`)

fields.name: design
fields.description: the study design and the data regime, as stated

fields.name: stated_limitation
fields.description: a limitation the authors themselves state

fields.name: open_question
fields.description: a question the authors themselves leave open

RP_CLAIMS.label: Claim inventory
RP_CLAIMS.purpose: Record every claim a paper makes or reports, with who holds it (the authors themselves, or earlier work the authors describe or criticise), what kind of claim it is, and the conditions the authors attach to it. A claim stays one claim: its qualifiers, scope and conditions stay with it.
RP_CLAIMS.instructions: Read all the text shown and report claims as records. A record's `field` is the kind of claim: empirical_finding (a result), interpretive_finding (a theme or interpretation drawn from qualitative material), theoretical_proposition (a proposition, an argument's conclusion, a proposed framework or reconceptualisation), methodological_claim (a claim about a method or measure), definition (a construct or distinction defined), claimed_contribution (what the paper says it adds), assumption (one the authors state), boundary_condition (where a claim is said not to hold), limitation (one the authors state), gap_statement (a gap or open question the authors identify). `type` is WHO HOLDS THE CLAIM according to the text: AUTHOR_OWN_CLAIM (the authors assert it as their own result or argument), AUTHOR_REPORTS_PRIOR_WORK (the authors describe what earlier work found or argued: `Smith (2020) argues ...`, `previous studies have shown ...`), AUTHOR_CRITIQUES_PRIOR_WORK (the authors dispute or qualify earlier work). A sentence that describes earlier work is not the authors' own claim, even in a sentence the authors agree with; and a paper may move from describing earlier work to arguing its own, so decide for each sentence. Never attribute a reported claim to the cited authors as if you had read them: you have read only this paper. Put the citation text you see (for example `Smith (2020)`) in `attributes.cited_works`. `quote` is the exact words of the claim. `value` restates the claim without adding anything the quote does not say. In `attributes` give only what the text states or what you must infer, and leave out what neither gives you: `constructs` (names of the ideas the claim is about), `scope` (population, setting, period, level_of_analysis), `premises`, `mechanism`, `boundary_conditions`, `direction` (for an empirical finding), `granularity` (ATOMIC if one proposition can be judged alone; COMPOUND if several are tied together: then list them in `components`, each with its own `conditions`, and keep the whole claim as one record), `cited_works`, `attribution_cue` (the words that show who holds the claim), `needs_deeper_reading` with a reason if the claim cannot be understood from this passage alone. If conditions or qualifiers sit in other sentences, give those sentences in `extra_quotes` (each an exact span, with a `role` of QUALIFIER, SUPPORTING_EVIDENCE, PREMISE, CONTEXT or BOUNDARY and `why` it is needed). Report each sentence once. Do not stop after a few claims: report all of them. Do not judge whether a claim is true, and do not complete a claim, a premise or a condition the text does not give.

fields.name: empirical_finding
fields.description: a result the paper reports or describes, with the population, period or estimand the sentence states

fields.name: interpretive_finding
fields.description: an interpretation, theme or pattern derived from qualitative material

fields.name: theoretical_proposition
fields.description: a proposition, the conclusion of an argument, a proposed framework or a reconceptualisation

fields.name: methodological_claim
fields.description: a claim about a method, a measure or a design choice

fields.name: definition
fields.description: a construct or a conceptual distinction as defined

fields.name: claimed_contribution
fields.description: what the paper says it contributes

fields.name: assumption
fields.description: an assumption that is stated

fields.name: boundary_condition
fields.description: where a claim is said not to hold, or to hold only under a stated condition

fields.name: limitation
fields.description: a limitation that is stated

fields.name: gap_statement
fields.description: a gap, tension or open question that is identified

RP_CLAIM_EVIDENCE.label: Evidence for one claim
RP_CLAIM_EVIDENCE.purpose: Given one claim of a paper, find in the text shown the sentences that bear on it: its conditions and qualifiers, the evidence offered for it, and the premises it needs.
RP_CLAIM_EVIDENCE.instructions: The line after the source title names ONE claim of this paper. Read the text shown and report only sentences that bear on that claim. `field` says how: qualifier (a condition or limit attached to the claim), supporting_evidence (a result, observation or argument the paper offers for the claim), premise (something the claim rests on), context (needed to read the claim correctly), boundary (where it is said not to hold). `quote` is the exact sentence. `value` says in a few words why the sentence bears on the claim. Report nothing that does not bear on the claim, and nothing the text does not say. If no sentence in the text shown bears on it, return no records and name that in `gaps`.

fields.name: qualifier
fields.description: a condition or limit the paper attaches to the claim

fields.name: supporting_evidence
fields.description: a result, observation or argument the paper offers for the claim

fields.name: premise
fields.description: something the claim rests on, as the paper states it

fields.name: context
fields.description: a sentence needed to read the claim correctly

fields.name: boundary
fields.description: where the paper says the claim does not hold
